title: Two Rising Runs Back to Back
statement:
You get an integer array nums and a length k. Look for two slices of length k that sit directly next to each other: one covering nums[a .. a + k − 1] and the next covering nums[a + k .. a + 2k − 1].

Return true if some start a makes both slices strictly increasing, and false otherwise. The step from the last value of the first slice to the first value of the second does not matter: it may go up, stay flat or go down.

examples.why: [1, 4, 6] and [2, 3, 8] are both strictly rising and start right after each other.
[1, 2, 3] and [4, 6, 7] both rise, but they are not adjacent. Every adjacent pair of length-3 slices contains a drop.
[1, 2] then [2, 3]. The flat step between the two slices is allowed, so you do not need one rising run of length 4.

hints: For a slice to be strictly increasing, every step inside it must go up. Which information about each position lets you answer that in O(1)?
Compute, for each index, the length of the strictly rising run that ends there. A slice ending at i rises exactly when that length is at least k.

Or walk the array once, tracking the length of the current rising run and the one just before it. Two adjacent slices fit if one run has length at least 2k, or two consecutive runs both have length at least k.

explain.intuition:
Split the array into maximal strictly rising runs: a new run starts every time a value fails to beat the one before it. Any strictly rising slice lies entirely inside one run.

So two adjacent rising slices can only appear in two ways. Either both lie in the same run, which then needs length at least 2k. Or the first slice ends exactly where a run ends and the second starts the next run, so both runs need length at least k. Tracking just the current run and the previous run while you scan checks both cases in one pass.
steps: Set prev = 0 (length of the previous run) and cur = 1 (length of the run ending at index 0).
For each i from 1: if nums[i] > nums[i − 1], extend the run with cur++. Otherwise the run breaks: prev = cur, cur = 1.
After each step, return true if cur ≥ 2k or min(prev, cur) ≥ k.
If the scan ends without a hit, return false.
pitfalls: Requiring one rising run of length 2k. The step between the two slices may be flat or a drop, as in [1, 2, 2, 3].
Accepting any two rising runs of length k, even far apart. They must be neighbours, as the second example shows.
Using ≥ instead of > for the rising test. Equal neighbours break a strictly increasing run.

solutions.title: Check every start position
solutions.idea: Try every start a and test both slices step by step.

solutions.title: Run lengths ending at each index
solutions.idea: run[i] is the length of the rising run ending at i. The slice ending at i rises when run[i] ≥ k, so check run[a + k − 1] and run[a + 2k − 1].

solutions.title: Current and previous run
solutions.idea: Scan once keeping the length of the current rising run and the one before it. One run of length 2k, or two neighbouring runs of length k, is enough.

followups: Return the largest k for which two adjacent rising slices exist. How does the run-length scan give that directly?
What if you need three adjacent rising slices instead of two?
